title: Cost-Aware Telemetry at Scale
summary: Observability data itself becomes a scaling and cost problem at large volume — sampling strategy and metric cardinality are design decisions, not something to leave to the monitoring team.

slides.markdown:
"Instrument everything" is good early advice and a bad long-term default. Past a certain scale, telemetry volume — traces, high-cardinality metrics, verbose logs — becomes a cost and infrastructure problem in its own right, sometimes rivaling the cost of the system it's monitoring.

This topic covers sampling strategy and metric cardinality as deliberate design decisions: what to keep at full fidelity, what to compress, and the one-label mistake that can 100x a metrics bill overnight.

slides.sectionTitle: Why "instrument everything" stops working once telemetry volume becomes its own bill
slides.markdown:
At low traffic, tracing 100% of requests and logging generously costs almost nothing — the volume is trivial. At high traffic, the same blanket policy scales linearly (or worse) with the system it's watching: a service handling 500,000 requests/sec generates telemetry at a scale that can genuinely rival the cost of the compute it's monitoring.

The mental shift needed at scale: telemetry isn't free observability, it's a dataset with its own storage, ingestion, and query costs — and like any dataset, it needs a retention and volume strategy instead of an unbounded "keep everything" default. This is exactly why sampling and cardinality control (next slides) become design decisions rather than afterthoughts.

slides.sectionTitle: Sampling strategies: head-based, tail-based, and adaptive sampling for traces
slides.markdown:
Building on [distributed tracing](distributed-tracing-design)'s head-based vs tail-based split: at real scale, a third option matters — **adaptive sampling**, which adjusts the sample rate dynamically based on current volume and what's already been captured, rather than using one fixed rate everywhere.

A fixed 1% head-based rate on a service doing 10 requests/sec versus one doing 100,000 requests/sec produces wildly different absolute trace volumes for the same relative sample. Adaptive sampling instead targets an absolute rate — say, "keep roughly 100 traces/sec regardless of total traffic" — so cost stays predictable even as traffic scales up or down, and low-traffic services still get meaningful coverage that a flat percentage would starve.

slides.markdown:
![Trace pipeline forking at the sampling decision stage](assets/trace-sampling-pipeline.svg)

The sampling decision point is the single place where cost gets controlled before data ever reaches expensive storage. Everything upstream (services emitting spans) stays unaware of the policy; everything downstream (storage, query, dashboards) only ever sees the already-reduced volume — which is what makes the sampling policy something you can tune independently, without touching instrumented services.

slides.sectionTitle: Cardinality explosions: how one high-cardinality label multiplies your metrics cost
slides.markdown:
A metric's **cardinality** is the number of distinct label-value combinations it produces. `http_requests_total{endpoint="/checkout", status="200"}` with 50 endpoints and 5 status codes is 250 time series — manageable. Add a `user_id` label, and with a million users that single metric explodes into a million-times-250 time series, because the metrics backend has to store and index every distinct combination separately.

This is a **cardinality explosion**, and it's the single most common way a metrics bill goes from reasonable to unsustainable overnight — the problem isn't the number of metrics, it's the number of *distinct combinations* any one metric's labels can produce, and unbounded fields (user IDs, request IDs, raw IPs) are the usual culprit.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: sampling to cut volume vs aggregating to cut cardinality — different problems, different fixes
slides.markdown:
| | Sampling | Aggregation (reducing cardinality) |
|---|---|---|
| Problem it solves | Too many events/traces overall | Too many distinct label combinations on one metric |
| Applies to | Traces, verbose logs | Metrics with unbounded or high-cardinality labels |
| Trade-off | Loses some individual events entirely | Loses per-value granularity (e.g. per-user) in exchange for a stable time-series count |
| Example fix | Trace 1% of requests, 100% of errors | Drop the `user_id` label; log it in traces/logs instead, where per-event detail is expected |

**How to decide:** if the issue is raw volume of similar events, sample. If the issue is one metric multiplying into too many time series because of a label, the fix is removing or bucketing that label — sampling a high-cardinality metric doesn't fix the cardinality, it just samples the explosion.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: adding a user-ID label to a metric and 100x'ing the time-series count overnight
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Adding a `user_id` label to this metric will help us debug per-user issues, and labels are cheap."

**Why it's wrong:** a label isn't cheap in isolation — its cost is multiplicative with every other label already on that metric, and a user ID has effectively unbounded cardinality. A metric with 250 time series before the change can become tens of millions after, since the metrics backend now stores a separate series for every user times every existing label combination, often overwhelming the backend or the bill within hours.

**Correct model:** never attach an unbounded field (user ID, request ID, raw IP, email) as a metric label. If per-user detail is genuinely needed, get it from traces or logs — both are built for high-cardinality, per-event data — and keep metrics reserved for bounded, aggregate dimensions.

slides.sectionTitle: Worked example: sizing a trace sampling rate against a real budget
slides.markdown:
A service handling 50,000 requests/sec, tracing 100% of them, generates 50,000 traces/sec — at a typical few KB per trace, that's on the order of 100-150 MB/sec of trace data, easily tens of terabytes per day, an infeasible ingestion and storage bill for most teams. Dropping to a flat 1% head-based sample brings that to 500 traces/sec, roughly 1-1.5 MB/sec, a completely different cost category and one most tracing backends handle comfortably.

The trade-off that number hides: at 1% sampling, a rare error occurring in 1 out of every 10,000 requests has only a 1-in-100 chance of being captured at all per occurrence, meaning it might take hundreds of occurrences before a trace of it exists to debug from. This is exactly why production systems combine a low baseline sample rate for normal traffic with a separate **100%-sample-on-error** rule — the volume math works because errors are rare, so tracing all of them costs little, while tracing all of the (vastly more common) successful requests would cost everything.

Sizing a sampling rate is a real capacity-planning exercise: pick a target ingestion volume your budget supports, work backward to the sample rate that hits it, then verify that rate still gives your on-call team enough error and slow-request coverage to actually debug incidents.

slides.sectionTitle: Log volume control: sampling by level and by content, not a blanket cut
slides.markdown:
Logs have their own version of the sampling problem, and a blanket "log less" policy is the wrong instrument for it, because different log levels carry very different debugging value per byte. A service emitting verbose `debug` logs on every request at high traffic can dwarf its `error` log volume by a factor of 1,000 or more, while carrying a fraction of the debugging value per line during an actual incident.

The standard split: sample `info`/`debug` logs aggressively (say, 1-5% in production, or disable `debug` entirely outside of active investigation), while keeping `warn`/`error` logs at or near 100%, since they're both rarer and disproportionately valuable when an incident is actually happening. Some teams add **dynamic log-level escalation** — temporarily raising a service's log verbosity to `debug` for a short window when an alert fires, capturing rich detail exactly when it's needed without paying that cost during normal operation.

The underlying principle is the same one driving trace sampling: the interesting, rare events (errors, active incidents) are cheap to capture at full fidelity because they're rare; the common, low-value events are what needs the volume cut, precisely because there are so many of them.
